title: The Psychology of Being Observed
author: The Mindful Manager
summary: Triggered by watching a calm, confident junior doctor become visibly hesitant the instant his supervising consultant entered the room, this piece uses Evaluation Apprehension Theory to explain a pattern the author recognizes in their own career: capable people underperforming specifically in front of senior figures, not because they lack skill but because the awareness of being judged consumes the attention that should be going to the task itself. The piece is careful to separate two related but distinct frameworks — Evaluation Apprehension explains why observed performance degrades (attention shifts from the task to self-monitoring and the observer's reaction), while Social Facilitation Theory and the Yerkes-Dodson Law explain when observation actually helps (simple, well-practiced tasks under moderate pressure) versus when it backfires (complex, unfamiliar, or creative work under high pressure). Its leadership prescriptions are concrete and low-cost: openly share your own mistakes to build psychological safety, explicitly state why you're observing a given interaction so it isn't read as a silent test, and periodically ask 'what would be most helpful from me here' rather than assuming your presence is neutral or automatically beneficial. The piece closes with a sharp reframe of what leadership success actually looks like — not how people perform while being watched, but how confidently they perform when the leader isn't in the room at all.
points: Uses a vivid clinical example — a confident junior doctor becoming visibly hesitant the instant his consultant walked in — to make evaluation apprehension concrete and immediate.
Distinguishes when observation helps from when it hurts: Social Facilitation Theory says it improves simple, well-practiced tasks but degrades complex or creative ones, per the Yerkes-Dodson Law.
Gives leaders a specific, low-cost fix: explicitly state why you're observing a given meeting or task, since unexplained observation defaults to feeling like a silent test.
Reframes the actual measure of good leadership: not how people perform while being watched, but how confidently they perform when the leader isn't in the room.
quotes: The doctor who had been calm moments before became hesitant. His movements were less certain and he suddenly looked like someone performing the procedure for the very first time.

Evaluation Apprehension Theory suggests that our performance changes in the presence of others because we're concerned about being socially evaluated... Instead of helping us perform better, that awareness quietly steals our attention.

This is supported by Social Facilitation Theory, which suggests that being observed can actually improve performance on simple or well-practised tasks because we become more alert and focused. However, when the task is complex, unfamiliar or requires creativity, that same attention can have the opposite effect.
That's one reason micromanagement so often backfires. Instead of increasing confidence, it increases evaluation apprehension. Instead of improving focus, it divides attention.
The measure of great leadership isn't how people perform when we're watching. It's how confidently they perform when we're not.
